title: Curiosity in the Classroom
author: Harriett Janetos and Jennifer Newman
summary: Harriett Janetos and Jennifer Newman make an extended case that Linguistic Phonics, the speech-to-print approach derived from Diane McGuinness, may teach foundational reading as effectively as traditional phonics but far more efficiently. Structured as a three-stop 'Magic School Bus' tour, the post first draws on Paul Kirschner's The Science of Education to warn against turning single findings into classroom commandments, then applies Tipton and Patton-Terry's 'engineering of reading' and its five Design Thinking steps to problems like getting students from word-level phonics to connected text. The second stop uses Carl Hendrick's argument about boundary conditions to contend that Linguistic Phonics organizes instruction within clear, knowable limits, starting from speech and phonemes, whereas Structured Literacy, Balanced Literacy, and Structured Word Inquiry blur those limits with rimes, syllable types, sight words, or early morphology. The final stop moves to practice, citing Marnie Ginsberg's short list of what must be taught explicitly, Miriam Fein's 'do this, not that' guidance, and a critical look at UFLI Foundations to separate need-to-do from nice-to-do activities. The authors frame the argument as a request to widen the instructional lens rather than adopt a program, insisting that practices gain or lose power depending on the instructional architecture around them.
points: The authors argue that similar phonics activities can have very different effects depending on the curriculum's overall architecture and core principles, so borrowing techniques is not enough.

Using Hendrick's boundary conditions, they claim teaching the code from speech to print reduces working memory load compared with grapheme-first phonics loaded with terminology like digraphs and blends.

McGuinness's 2002 'Prototype' serves as a predictor: start with phonemes, teach a transparent basic code before alternatives, integrate reading and spelling, and avoid sight-word memorization and syllable types.
Marnie Ginsberg's 'three S' domains (structure, strategies, systems practice) show how Linguistic Phonics exits explicit declarative instruction early to leave time for connected text.
A line-by-line look at UFLI Foundations questions whether phonemic awareness without letters, onset-rime chains, and heavy terminology are essential or merely add cognitive burden.
quotes: The instructional architecture and core principles of a Linguistic Phonics approach may increase the probability of effective and efficient learning of foundational reading skills. Similar activities and techniques used across programs may have less impact when inserted into curricular designs that differ in overall structure and core principles.

This is precisely what McGuinness offers with Linguistic Phonics. The content we teach (the code itself) doesn’t change, but how we perceive it does. Where Structured Literacy sees a duck, Linguistic Phonics sees a rabbit!

Unlike the traditional print-oriented phonics of Structured Literacy (SL), Balanced Literacy (BL), or Structured Word Inquiry (SWI), Linguistic Phonics designs instruction around clear, knowable boundaries that give novice learners a logical, coherent, and manageable framework. Within this framework, they efficiently discover how the code works at its entry level. Although this may seem like a distinction without a difference, when we organize instruction around speech—what’s known—and then attach letters—what’s unknown—we are anchoring our instruction in familiar territory.

Traditional phonics can place a heavy burden on a beginner’s working memory by introducing the code through graphemes rather than through speech. Taught backwards, from print to speech, the code’s relationship to spoken language and its underlying boundaries can become obscured.

The paradox is that starting with simple, knowable boundaries for learning the English alphabetic code builds the knowledge and skills needed to go beyond them to perceive the less knowable boundaries that define the code at its expert layers. Having these clear boundaries at the outset is what opens awareness and access in the long run.

Linguistic Phonics escapes from domains 1 and 2 early, but it can take far longer for traditional phonics to do so. Efficiency doesn’t mean rushing through phonics. It means being thoughtful about what we teach, why we teach it, how much explanation is necessary, and when students are ready to use their knowledge in authentic reading and writing tasks.

Teaching traditional phonics, including UFLI, is like keeping the training wheels on a child's bike too long. Linguistic Phonics offers them a pedal-less bike to push with their feet so they learn to balance faster and have time for reading connected text and writing.

We know that an understanding of the boundary conditions of our principles helps us decide what to leave out of our instruction as much as what to leave in. We streamline our lessons because we know that when it comes to phonics instruction, less can be more. But the goal is not simply to do fewer things. It is to make sure what we do is coherent, purposeful, and aligned with the way learning works.
